title: Submarine production rate 'flat', US Congressional report author says
transcript:
Host: Defence Minister Richard Marles has criticized the US Congressional Budget Office over reports that says that AUKUS pact will decrease the number of attack submarines available to the US Navy.
Host: The report found the US submarine industrial base is struggling to meet the Navy's demands with the cost of its new fleet blowing out by billions of dollars.
Host: Richard Marles questioned those findings on the ABC's Insiders program yesterday.
Richard Marles: That production rate is definitely a critical part of it.
Host: Is it improving that production?
Richard Marles: It is absolutely improving. Because this report suggests it's still I think you're you're going to see people continue to say that they're wrong.
Host: The US Congressional office?
Richard Marles: Yes, they are wrong.
Richard Marles: Um the the production rate in the United States is absolutely increasing.
Host: That's Defence Minister Richard Marles speaking with David Spears yesterday.
Host: Well, Dr Eric Gbs is a senior analyst for Naval Forces and weapons at the US Congressional Budget Office.
Host: He authored the report on ship building capacity and joins me now.
Host: Eric Gbs, welcome to Radio National Breakfast.
Eric Gbs: Well, thank you for having me.
Host: The Australian Defence Minister is questioning the findings of this report.
Host: Have you got it wrong here?
Eric Gbs: Well, the report is mainly about an independent analysis of the Navy's 30-year ship building plan.
Eric Gbs: So most of what I write about there, which is a report required by US law, um does an independent cost estimate look on the Navy's ship programs.
Eric Gbs: I discussed AUKUS and the ship building industrial base in the report.
Eric Gbs: And uh what I focused on was the fact that given the given what the United States Navy wishes to purchase over the next 10 to you know, 10 to 20 years and what we've been building now, there's going to be a lot more tonnage that's going to be required to be produced by the US industrial base.
Eric Gbs: And um that is going to that is a result is going to be a challenge and that is before any replacement submarines are incorporated into that.
Eric Gbs: So my simple argument was, look, we've increased submarine tonnage production by doubling it over the past 10 years.
Eric Gbs: It's got to go up another 50% over the next 5 to 10 years.
Eric Gbs: That's an enormous challenge for the ship building industrial base to be able to meet.
Host: How important do you think it is to have these you know, difficult conversations about how production is going so that problems down the track can be better foreseen?
Eric Gbs: I think it's important that for the US Congress and anybody interested in the in in the report that that CBO is required to write, just have simply the best factual information available.
Eric Gbs: And that's all that I'm trying to do.
Eric Gbs: I'm not saying AUKUS is a good idea or a bad idea.
Eric Gbs: I'm that's not CBO's purview.
Eric Gbs: We don't make policy recommendations, we simply provide uh analysis and information to the Congress so they can be as informed as they possible as well informed as they possibly can in order to make the decisions that that confront them on AUKUS and other ship Navy ship building programs.
Host: Eric, given the research and analysis that you've undertaken in this role, do you think it is likely that the AUKUS submarines for Australia will be completed within the time frame expected?
Eric Gbs: Well, it's right now that's honestly unclear because the Navy ship building program, the program that they proposed in their in their May report, it's similar to several previous reports where they do not incorporate into that plan the replacement submarines for the AUKUS program.
Eric Gbs: So the question becomes, does the United States transfer the submarines, sell the submarines to Australia in the 2030s on schedule and then just allow for the fact that the replacements are going to come later?
Eric Gbs: Because it is not it is not really possible under the current industrial base conditions to have those replacement submarines built before at least the first one transfers in the early 2030s and frankly even before the second one transfers in the mid 2030s.
Eric Gbs: The industrial base is just not producing submarines fast enough to do that and, you know, the current production rate based on the data that I have as of June of this year, that's the latest data I have available to me is that the production rate is has been flat.
Eric Gbs: It's been flat for the past two years on average, which is actually even a little bit less than what it was over the last five years.
Host: Richard Marles, the Australian Defence Minister says production rate isn't the only important factor to consider and that sustainment and maintenance are also critical to the delivery of AUKUS.
Host: What do you think?
Eric Gbs: Well, there is an important element to that that with US submarines as part of the AUKUS agreement would be operating from Australia and that that the Australian industrial base and Australian government would be helping to maintain those submarines.
Eric Gbs: That does serve a sort of a counter balancing factor in the sense that submarines then can get uh fixed and repaired and sent back to the fleet faster than they would if those submarines were being maintained and repaired in the United States.
Eric Gbs: So that element can you know, perhaps offset the fact that maybe the United States won't have as many submarines as it planned uh under the AUKUS agreement at least initially until those replacement submarines are eventually built.
Host: You're listening to Radio National Breakfast.
Host: My guest is uh senior analyst from the US Congressional Budget Office Dr.
Host: Eric Gbs.
Host: What impact, Eric, is the war in Iran had on capabilities and production rate for the US Navy?
Eric Gbs: Um in terms of production rate, it would really have have not much effect at all on on the US Navy because ships take a long time to build and what's going on in in Iran is is not affecting sort of new ship construction.
Host: Where it is going to have an effect is the fact that with so much of the US Navy deployed overseas and operating, the uh uh shipyards in the United States that perform maintenance on its on its ships, particularly its surface ships, um don't have a lot of work right now.
Eric Gbs: And so they're going to be expecting a lot of work in the future when the when this operation winds down.
Eric Gbs: So they're going to go through a bit of a feast and famine cycle where you know the shipyards need work now, they don't have as much as they'd like and there's going to be a lot to do later on.
Eric Gbs: So deferred maintenance is going to be an issue that the US Navy is going to have to manage for for quite a few years to come.
Host: Are there increase maintenance needs as well when uh the US fleet is involved in a drawn-out conflict?
Eric Gbs: It that is sometimes hard to tell.
Eric Gbs: As a general rule, you do see more in more maintenance is required on a ship that is deployed longer than what it when what is initially planned for on the part of the US Navy.
Eric Gbs: So if we typically plan for seven-month deployments and it's an 11-month deployment, well then there's going to be more maintenance that's going to be needed to be done on that ship.
Eric Gbs: But it's not necessarily clear that that's going to be a whole lot more than what whatever what would have been required in any event.
Eric Gbs: But the problem becomes that it's deferred, a lot of ships are deferred, so then it things are going to get stacked up um you know down the road as a result of that.
Host: The sale of submarines to Australia could shrink the US attack submarine force through to 2060.
Host: What options are open to the United States when it comes to increasing its naval forces when considering AUKUS?
Eric Gbs: Well, the United States Navy is going through uh an industry in in ship building industry in the United States is going through a number of efforts to increase the rate of attack submarine production in particular.
Eric Gbs: Uh they're distributing more work to other shipyards, uh what they call federated ship building or distributed uh distributed ship building.
Eric Gbs: So that is efforts to try to increase the rate of uh attack submarine production.
Eric Gbs: There are other ship building programs that are doing similar things and other ships could be purchased, not submarines, uh that could do can be able to contribute to the effort.
Eric Gbs: Um, but in the case of submarines, even with those efforts involved, it takes a long time to build a submarine.
Eric Gbs: You're not going to get a very rapid acceleration with with the investment that's being occurring in the United States in the ship building industry, submarines in particular, including Australian investment, we should overtime see a a a gradual rise in the production of those attack submarines, but it's not something that's going to happen quickly or happen fast.
Eric Gbs: The CNO that was nominated in 2022 said we would get to a much higher rate of production by 2026.
Eric Gbs: Uh the CNO who was nominated and got the job in 2026 said, well, we should see a much higher rate of submarine production by 2030.
Eric Gbs: So that four-year window has kind of moved forward in time and we have not seen a lot of progress yet, although there are some promising signs.
Host: Eric Gbs, thank you for joining me.
Eric Gbs: Thank you for having me.
